subject: Renal
vignette: A 45-year-old man undergoes urinalysis as part of a routine physical. Microscopic examination of the sediment shows cylindrical elements with parallel sides and rounded ends. The laboratory technician notes that these elements are found in virtually every type of cast, from hyaline to red cell casts. The physician wants to explain what gives all urinary casts their structural framework.
question: Which of the following is the primary matrix component shared by all urinary casts?

options.text: Albumin that has precipitated within the tubular lumen
Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein (uromodulin) secreted by renal tubular cells
Cross-linked type IV collagen shed from the glomerular basement membrane
Fibrin polymer deposited as a result of glomerular inflammation
Immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones protein)

explanation_correct: All urinary casts share a matrix composed primarily of Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein, also called uromodulin, which is secreted by renal tubular cells and normally helps prevent urinary tract infections. Cells or debris become embedded in this proteinaceous matrix as it gels within the tubular lumen, producing the different cast types. Recognizing this common matrix explains why a cast, wherever it is seen, implies a process originating within the nephron rather than the lower urinary tract.

explanation_incorrect.A: Albumin is a small protein that can leak into urine in proteinuria, but it is not the structural matrix of casts; uromodulin is the principal framework protein.
explanation_incorrect.C: Type IV collagen is a structural component of the glomerular basement membrane that is abnormal in Alport syndrome; it does not form the matrix of ordinary casts.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fibrin can be incorporated into the crescents of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, not into the matrix of routine urinary casts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Bence Jones light chains can form pathologic casts in myeloma kidney, but these are a special deposit, not the universal Tamm-Horsfall matrix.

educationalObjective: All urinary casts are built on a Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein (uromodulin) matrix secreted by renal tubular cells.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after a sore throat. Blood pressure is 155/95 mm Hg, BUN is 32 mg/dL, and creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 2+ protein, and microscopic examination reveals dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts.
question: The presence of red blood cell casts in this patient's urine most specifically indicates which of the following?

options.text: Acute cystitis involving the bladder mucosa
Lower urinary tract bleeding from a kidney stone
Nephrotic syndrome resulting from podocyte injury
Glomerulonephritis or a hypertensive emergency
Acute tubular necrosis from ischemic injury

explanation_correct: RBC casts form when erythrocytes leak through a damaged glomerular basement membrane and become trapped in the Tamm-Horsfall matrix within the tubule. Their presence localizes hematuria to the glomerulus and is a hallmark of glomerulonephritis; they are also seen in hypertensive emergencies. The dysmorphic red cells, elevated BUN and creatinine, and hypertension in this vignette are classic nephritic features consistent with infection-related glomerulonephritis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acute cystitis produces pyuria without casts; it is a lower urinary tract process and does not generate red cell casts.
explanation_incorrect.B: Kidney stones cause hematuria without casts because bleeding arises in the lower urinary tract rather than at the glomerulus.
explanation_incorrect.C: Nephrotic syndrome is due to podocyte damage and produces fatty casts and oval fat bodies, not red cell casts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acute tubular necrosis is associated with muddy brown granular casts rather than red cell casts.

educationalObjective: RBC casts signal glomerular bleeding and are characteristic of glomerulonephritis or hypertensive emergency.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 35-year-old man has painless gross hematuria. CT urogram reveals a 3-cm mass in the bladder wall; urine microscopy shows many red blood cells but no casts. A separate 24-year-old woman with dysuria and suprapubic pain has pyuria but no casts on microscopy.
question: Which of the following best explains the absence of casts in both of these patients?

options.text: Their hematuria and pyuria arise from the lower urinary tract, not from glomeruli or tubules
Both patients have severe renal impairment that prevents cast formation
Tamm-Horsfall protein secretion is absent in lower urinary tract disease
Casts dissolve rapidly in alkaline urine and are never seen in outpatients
Neither patient has inflammation, so no cellular elements can be incorporated

explanation_correct: Casts form only within the renal tubules, so their presence indicates a glomerular or renal tubular source of hematuria or pyuria. Bladder cancer and kidney stones produce hematuria without casts, and acute cystitis produces pyuria without casts, because these are lower urinary tract processes. Thus the absence of casts in both patients correctly points away from the kidney parenchyma.

explanation_incorrect.B: Neither patient has evidence of advanced renal impairment; BUN and creatinine would be expected to be abnormal if that were the explanation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tamm-Horsfall mucoprotein is still secreted by renal tubular cells in lower tract disease; casts do not form because blood and pus cells never enter the tubules.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cast stability does vary with urine pH and osmolality, but it is false that casts are never seen in outpatients, and this does not explain the localized findings.
explanation_incorrect.E: Both patients do have bleeding or inflammation: bladder cancer is a source of gross hematuria and cystitis is inflammatory, yet neither produces casts.

educationalObjective: Hematuria or pyuria without casts localizes the process to the lower urinary tract (eg, bladder cancer, stones, cystitis).

subject: Renal
vignette: A 52-year-old renal transplant recipient presents 3 weeks after surgery with fever, graft tenderness, and a rise in serum creatinine from 1.2 to 2.4 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows leukocytes and leukocyte casts. Another patient with an uncomplicated bladder infection has pyuria but no casts.
question: Leukocyte casts in these patients point to which of the following processes?

options.text: Lower urinary tract infection confined to the bladder lumen
Glomerular basement membrane injury from anti-GBM antibodies
Tubulointerstitial inflammation, such as acute pyelonephritis or transplant rejection
Podocyte injury with loss of the charge barrier
Ischemic injury to the proximal tubule from hypotension

explanation_correct: WBC casts indicate that leukocytes have migrated into the tubular lumen, which occurs with tubulointerstitial inflammation. Classic causes include acute pyelonephritis and acute transplant rejection, both of which inflame the interstitium and tubules. The contrast with simple cystitis, which gives pyuria without casts, reinforces that WBC casts localize inflammation to the kidney itself.

explanation_incorrect.A: Uncomplicated cystitis produces pyuria without casts because the bladder lumen is not part of the tubular compartment where casts form.
explanation_incorrect.B: Anti-GBM injury (Goodpasture syndrome) causes RBC casts and linear immunofluorescence, not WBC casts.
explanation_incorrect.D: Podocyte injury causes nephrotic syndrome with fatty casts, not leukocyte casts.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ischemic proximal tubular injury produces muddy brown granular casts (ATN), not WBC casts.

educationalObjective: WBC casts indicate tubulointerstitial inflammation, classically acute pyelonephritis or transplant rejection.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 60-year-old man develops severe hypotension during abdominal surgery owing to massive blood loss. Over the next 48 hours his urine output falls and his creatinine rises from 1.0 to 3.0 mg/dL. Urine microscopy shows pigmented, granular casts with a muddy brown appearance and evidence of tubular injury. FENa is 2.8%.
question: Which of the following cast types is most characteristic of the renal lesion in this patient?

options.text: Fatty casts with Maltese cross birefringence
Broad waxy casts
Red blood cell casts
Leukocyte casts
Granular 'muddy brown' casts

explanation_correct: Ischemic acute tubular necrosis results from prolonged renal hypoperfusion and causes sloughing of necrotic tubular epithelial cells into the lumen. These cells and their debris become embedded in the uromodulin matrix, producing the muddy brown granular casts that are the histologic signature of ATN. The high FENa above 2% distinguishes this intrinsic renal injury from prerenal azotemia, in which only hyaline casts may be seen.

explanation_incorrect.A: Fatty casts with Maltese cross birefringence are seen in nephrotic syndrome due to lipiduria, not in ischemic tubular injury.
explanation_incorrect.B: Broad waxy casts are a feature of advanced chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease, not acute ATN.
explanation_incorrect.C: RBC casts imply glomerular bleeding from glomerulonephritis, not tubular necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: WBC casts indicate tubulointerstitial inflammation such as pyelonephritis, which is not the mechanism here.

educationalObjective: Muddy brown granular casts are the hallmark of acute tubular necrosis.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 9-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of periorbital edema and frothy urine. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein, and microscopic examination of the sediment under polarized light reveals refractile lipid-laden cells that produce a 'Maltese cross' pattern. Serum albumin is 1.9 g/dL and cholesterol is 320 mg/dL.
question: These oval fat bodies with a Maltese cross appearance are most consistent with which of the following?

options.text: Acute pyelonephritis
Nephrotic syndrome
Acute tubular necrosis
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
End-stage renal disease

explanation_correct: Fatty casts and oval fat bodies are lipid-laden tubular cells or casts that, under polarized light, show the characteristic Maltese cross birefringence. They are a classic finding in nephrotic syndrome, where heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia trigger compensatory hepatic lipogenesis and hypercholesterolemia, leading to lipiduria. The frothy urine, severe proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia in this child, likely from minimal change disease, complete the picture.

explanation_incorrect.A: Acute pyelonephritis is associated with WBC casts, not fatty casts or lipiduria.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acute tubular necrosis produces muddy brown granular casts rather than fatty casts.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis produces red cell casts and crescents, not oval fat bodies.
explanation_incorrect.E: End-stage renal disease is associated with broad waxy casts, not lipid-laden oval fat bodies.

educationalObjective: Fatty casts and oval fat bodies with Maltese cross birefringence are characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.

subject: Renal
vignette: A 68-year-old man with long-standing diabetic nephropathy has a creatinine of 6.8 mg/dL and requires dialysis planning; his urine sediment shows broad casts with a waxy, refractile appearance. In contrast, a healthy 22-year-old woman has a few hyaline casts on urinalysis after a marathon and a day of dehydration, with normal renal function.
question: Which of the following statements best interprets these two findings?

options.text: Waxy casts indicate acute glomerulonephritis; hyaline casts are always pathologic
Both cast types are specific for nephrotic syndrome
Hyaline casts indicate end-stage renal disease; waxy casts are a normal finding after exercise
Waxy casts suggest end-stage renal disease/chronic kidney disease, whereas hyaline casts are nonspecific and can be normal with dehydration or exercise
Waxy casts are pathognomonic of acute tubular necrosis; hyaline casts indicate lower urinary tract infection

explanation_correct: Broad waxy casts form in dilated, scarred tubules with markedly reduced flow and are a hallmark of advanced chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease, matching this patient's diabetes and need for dialysis. Hyaline casts, by contrast, are acellular, nonspecific, and may be seen in healthy people after dehydration, strenuous exercise, or diuretic therapy. Thus the two cast types carry very different implications despite both being proteinaceous.

explanation_incorrect.A: Waxy casts are not specific for acute glomerulonephritis, which gives RBC casts, and hyaline casts are frequently a normal finding rather than always pathologic.
explanation_incorrect.B: Nephrotic syndrome is associated with fatty casts and oval fat bodies, not with this waxy-versus-hyaline pattern.
explanation_incorrect.C: This reverses the associations: hyaline casts are not a marker of end-stage disease, and waxy casts are not a normal post-exercise finding.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acute tubular necrosis gives muddy brown granular casts, and lower urinary tract infection does not produce casts at all; neither claim here is correct.

educationalObjective: Waxy casts indicate advanced CKD/ESRD, whereas hyaline casts are nonspecific and may be normal with dehydration, exercise, or diuretics.
